preamble: Reduction to schwa (ə) is the most common fate for any vowel in an unstressed syllable. The vowel 'a' loses its distinct low back quality and moves toward a neutral, central position in the mouth, requiring minimal articulatory effort.

examples.note: Unstressed first 'a' reduces to schwa in word-initial unstressed position
Final unstressed 'a' often reduces to a near-schwa

ATR vowel harmony: in Ateso, the low vowel /a/ in suffixes behaves as an underlying [-ATR] vowel; when a [+ATR] root triggers harmony, /a/ centralizes toward [ə]. The reduction reflects the interaction of ATR harmony with the neutral low vowel, which lacks a [+ATR] counterpart at the low position.

Nuer vowel system organizes vowels into modal/breathy pairs; the breathy schwa [ə̤] is a phonologized reduction of /a/ in breathy-phonation contexts. [ə̤] is the only schwa in the system and lacks a modal counterpart, representing the endpoint of vowel reduction under breathy voice.

In Central Atlas Tamazight, short /a/ in unstressed non-final syllables reduces to schwa [ə]. Schwa in Tamazight fills syllabic positions where full vowels are deleted under prosodic pressure; it is a non-moraic segment and does not participate in vowel harmony. This epenthetic/reductive schwa is distinct from the full vowels /a/, /i/, /u/.

Tashlhiyt (Tachelhit, southern Morocco) is exceptional among Berber languages in allowing words with no full vowels. Short /a/ that would become schwa in other Berber varieties is fully deleted in Tashlhiyt, yielding consonantal syllables. The occasional transitional schwa between consonants is phonetically present but not phonologically underlying.
Word-final *a is reduced to [ə] in standard Balinese, while the spelling keeps ⟨a⟩; Bali Aga dialects keep [a].
